decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding correctly classify the study as a replication collecting new participant data to re-test Roelofs et al. (2010). decisions.quote: Apart from arising in response to physical stressors, freezing can also occur in response to social threats. Specifically, Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins ( 2010 ) showed freezing in response to angry faces, suggesting that freezing is a generic threat response (see also Hagenaars et al., 2014a , b ). This is important because freezing in response to social situations has several practical implications ranging from the treatment of psychological trauma (Kozlowska, Walker, McLean, & Carrive, 2015 ) to improving the quality of social interactions (Mendes, Blascovich, Hunter, Lickel, & Jost, 2007 ). Given the important theoretical and practical consequences of freezing in response to social stress, together with the fact that Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ) is the only study showing freezing in response to social threat, the current study aimed to replicate Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ).
decisions.reason: Shipped row 2009 and blind target_index 0 both correctly identify the replicated original study as Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins (2010), 'Facing freeze: Social threat induces bodily freeze in humans' (Psychological Science, 21, 1575-1581; DOI: 10.1177/0956797610384746). Row 2009 was only left unpaired in the follow-up snapshot because shipped row 422 was a duplicate entry for the same replication that originally had erroneous metadata and was resolved to target_index 0 in the prior round.

decisions.reason: Both shipped row 2009 and blind coding classify the record as a replication. The study collected new heart-rate and state-anxiety data from an independent sample of 60 Dutch student participants (final N = 54) to re-test the findings of Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins (2010).

decisions.quote: To conclude, the current research has largely replicated the freezing-to-social-threat effect initially demonstrated by Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ). We hope our work strengthens the confidence in the effect and paves the way for further research and applications in the context of (social) threat and physiology.

previous_decisions.quote: Indeed, in our study, the effect is marginal and we do not replicate the negative correlation between heart rate and STAI in the angry block. While our findings are not completely in line with Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ), they support the notion that people show physiological signs of freezing in response to social threat.
previous_decisions.reason: The authors explicitly set out to test both whether viewing angry faces lowers heart rate relative to neutral/happy faces and whether this effect is modulated by state anxiety. While they found lower heart rate in the angry block (with marginal state-anxiety modulation only after excluding an outlier) and note in the conclusion that the study 'largely replicated the freezing-to-social-threat effect', they explicitly state in the Abstract, Results, and Discussion that they 'do not replicate the negative correlation between heart rate and STAI in the angry block' and that 'our findings are not completely in line with Roelofs et al. ( 2010 )'. Under the codebook, a tested finding explicitly contrasted with the original cannot be omitted from the verdict, making the outcome mixed.
